events.title: The Battle of the Winwaed
events.shortBlurb: By a rain-swollen river in the north, the Christian Oswiu overthrew the pagan Penda, and, Bede says, heathen Mercia turned to Christ…
body: Penda of Mercia, the last great pagan king among the English, had slain the Christian kings Edwin of Northumbria at Hatfield in 633 and Oswald at Maserfield in 642. In 655 he invaded Bernicia at the head of a great confederate host and besieged Bamburgh, threatening to undo the Christian ascendancy of the north.

Oswiu of Bernicia, offering treasure for peace in vain, vowed that if God granted him victory he would dedicate his infant daughter Ælfflæd to perpetual virginity and give twelve estates for the founding of monasteries. On 15 November 655, in the district of Loidis near Leeds, by the river Winwæd swollen with heavy rain, the armies met. Penda and some thirty allied leaders fell, and Bede records that "many more were drowned in the flight than destroyed by the sword."

Bede reckoned the battle the effective end of Anglo-Saxon paganism: Mercia and its neighbours received the Christian faith, and Penda's own baptized son Peada ruled the southern part. Oswiu kept his vow, and his daughter entered the monastery of Abbess Hilda, later removed to Whitby. The exact site of the river is disputed.

sources.text: Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English People, Book III (public-domain translation)
